before: **Portfolio holdings below 15% (§ 50j).** Where a treaty cuts German tax on dividends below 15% for a shareholder that is not a company holding at least 10% (for example the US pension fund at 0%, or the Dutch pension fund and UK pension scheme at 10%), the refund needs the recipient to have been the beneficial owner for 45 days within 45 days either side of the due date, carrying at least 70% of the risk of a fall in value, and not to pass the dividend on (§ 50j EStG). The tests in § 50j(1)–(3) do not apply if, at receipt, the recipient has been the economic owner of the shares or participation certificates continuously for at least one year (§ 50j(4) sentence 2); the FIFO rule in § 50j(2) sentence 2 still applies.
after: **Portfolio relief below 15% (§ 50j).** For the stated § 43(1) no. 1a/corresponding foreign-custody income where the treaty tax is below 15%, the § 50j(4) corporate exclusion requires a limited-liability foreign capital company directly holding at least one tenth of nominal capital in the specified unlimited-taxable German capital company, subject at home to income/profit tax without exemption; not every company with 10% qualifies. Otherwise test continuous economic ownership for 45 days within 45 days before/after the due date, at least 70% net downside risk including offsetting claims and related-person hedges, and no obligation to compensate another person wholly or predominantly, directly or indirectly, for the capital income. A voluntary distribution is not by itself that obligation. The tests in § 50j(1)–(3) do not apply if, at receipt, the recipient has been the economic owner of the shares or participation certificates continuously for at least one year (§ 50j(4) sentence 2); the FIFO rule in § 50j(2) sentence 2 still applies. Actual below-15% treaty entitlement and all other refund gates remain separate.

before: **Refund amount on a treaty dividend.** Refund = tax withheld − treaty limit × gross dividend. For a 15% treaty: 26.375% − 15% = 11.375% of the gross. This holds where the treaty's covered taxes include the solidarity surcharge. Austria, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Spain, the UK, Ireland and Poland list German taxes "including the supplements levied thereon" (art. 2); Switzerland and France cover taxes levied "also in the form of surcharges" (art. 2(1), art. 1(2)). Italy and the US do not expressly name supplements; their later-similar-tax clauses are Italy art. 2(4) and US art. 2(2). Czech Republic art. 2(3)(a) expressly names the corporation-tax Ergänzungsabgabe; whether the current solidarity surcharge falls within that wording or the later-similar-tax clause in art. 2(5) is not separately established here.
after: **Refund amount on a treaty dividend.** Once actual tax remittance and every entitlement/procedure gate are established, refund = tax withheld/remitted minus treaty limit × gross dividend. For a 15% treaty with combined tax/surcharge coverage: 26.375% − 15% = 11.375% of gross. Austria, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Spain, the UK, Ireland and Poland expressly include supplements, and Switzerland/France cover surcharge forms as stated in their tax articles. **Selected combined-text interpretation for Italy, the US and Czech Republic:** their income/corporation-tax and later identical or substantially similar additional/replacement-tax clauses cover the current surcharge on that income/corporation tax, so apply the treaty cap to core tax plus Soli together. Italy art. 2(4) and US art. 2(2) give the later-tax clauses; Czech art. 2(3)(a) expressly includes the corporation-tax Ergänzungsabgabe and art. 2(5) covers later similar additional/replacement taxes. SolzG § 3(1) nos. 5/6 ties current Soli to the same capital/§ 50a tax. This is a labelled own-primary interpretation, not a separately retained BZSt country-practice confirmation; the Czech comparison below uses it.
